title: AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field
gist: AWS launched Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in EKS pod, ECS task or EC2 workload in its own Firecracker microVM with a separate guest kernel, enabled on EKS via a single runtimeClassName (isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox), at no extra charge and aimed first at untrusted coding-agent code. Trade-offs include no GPU passthrough, capped density, SMT penalties, and confidentiality guarantees that depend on actually verifying attestation.

insights.claim: AWS Nitro Sandboxes run each opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight VM with a separate guest kernel carved from a running EC2 instance, enabled on Amazon EKS by setting runtimeClassName to isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hardware-isolated multi-tenancy becomes a one-line default on AWS, lowering the barrier to running untrusted code on shared Kubernetes nodes.

insights.claim: AWS offers Nitro Sandboxes in all commercial regions at no additional charge and positions them first for coding agents, then multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agentic coding workloads are now a primary design target for cloud isolation products, pressuring third-party sandbox startups that charge for the same capability.
insights.quote: Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.
insights.locator: The feature is available in all commercial regions

insights.claim: AWS points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted microVM in about two seconds.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cold-start latency for per-task VMs is the key UX hurdle for agent platforms; warm pools are the standard mitigation.

insights.claim: Under the hood, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process launches a Firecracker microVM with hardware-assisted virtualization; an in-VM agent runs containers via its own containerd, communicating over virtio and vsock, so sandboxes share neither kernel nor memory mappings with the host or each other.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Reuses the Lambda/Fargate Firecracker stack inside customer EKS nodes, deepening AWS's vertical isolation moat.

insights.claim: Isolated mode trusts the parent instance, so kubectl exec and logs still work, while confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted: a Cedar policy pins image digests and config, exec is denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures image and policy into PCRs, and KMS releases secrets only to matching measurements.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Confidential computing is being productized for ordinary Kubernetes pods, relevant for regulated and data-sensitive AI workloads.

insights.claim: Confidential mode's guarantees are incomplete unless a KMS policy or external verifier actually checks the PCR attestation measurements.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Security buyers must configure attestation verification; misconfiguration risk is a likely source of future incidents and tooling demand.
insights.quote: the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete.

insights.claim: AWS Container Hero Sandip Das notes isolated mode protection only runs one way: a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, write the pod's /etc/hosts, and mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Isolated mode protects the host from the pod, not the pod from the host; it is not a substitute for confidential mode in hostile-operator threat models.
insights.locator: Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero

insights.claim: Sandip Das advises treating AWS's near-native performance claim as a vendor claim and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency; prerequisites include Kubernetes 1.36+, Nitro Enclaves-enabled launch templates and Pod Identity rather than IRSA.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Adoption friction and unverified performance may slow uptake; independent benchmarks are the watch item.

insights.claim: Nitro Sandboxes do not support GPU or device passthrough at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: GPU-bound AI inference/training cannot yet get microVM isolation on AWS, leaving a gap for GPU-capable sandboxing (e.g. gVisor CUDA support).
insights.locator: The constraints are on the considerations page

insights.claim: Sandbox density is capped: total sandbox vCPUs and sandbox count may each not exceed five times the node vCPU count (halved on CPU-overcommit types), e.g. a 4-vCPU node fits twenty 1-vCPU or five 4-vCPU sandboxes.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Density caps translate into more EC2 instances per sandboxed workload, i.e. incremental compute revenue for AWS.

insights.claim: On x86 instances with simultaneous multithreading, core scheduling prevents two sandboxes sharing sibling threads, leaving roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable, whereas Graviton with one thread per core is unaffected.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sandboxed workloads structurally favor Graviton over SMT x86 instances, a tailwind for AWS's in-house Arm silicon versus Intel/AMD.

insights.claim: GKE Sandbox has offered a gVisor RuntimeClass since 2019 (sub-200 ms start, CUDA on some GPUs) and a microVM class on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor with fixed 250 mCPU/130 MiB per-pod overhead, 1-2 s startup and no GPU support; AWS chose the VM approach and expresses overhead as density and threads.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers are converging on runtime-class sandboxing; Google keeps a GPU-capable edge via gVisor, a differentiator for AI-agent workloads needing GPUs.
insights.locator: The nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox

insights.claim: On EC2, Nitro Sandboxes support Amazon Linux and Firecracker natively, with patches for other VMMs, but snapshot, restore and live migration are unavailable.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Lack of snapshot/restore limits fast-fork patterns some agent platforms rely on.
insights.locator: On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker
